beats.narration_text: The instructions define three modes. Help explains the sheet. Quiz gives one question and waits for your answer. Exam produces a complete twenty-question practice paper. The real exam is private and is not in this project.

props.title: Source excerpt · Three modes
lines: 1. **Help**: say what is on the exam, explain a topic, or make
the student a cheat sheet. 2. **Quiz**: give one question at a
time, and show the answer only after the student has answered.
3. **Exam**: write a full 20-question practice exam the student
can print, with the answer key only when they ask for it.  Your
only source for what is on the exam is the Project file **EXAM-
CHEAT-SHEET.md**. Read it before you answer anything about the
exam.

beats.narration_text: The knowledge sheet controls the scope. The updated sheet now includes Professor Bear's correction: know what physically based rendering is, and why it matters. Detailed P B R techniques and experience with a No-Bake system are not required. Game artificial intelligence remains outside this midterm. Always load the current sheet before generating practice.

props.title: Updated knowledge · PBR at a general level
lines: PBR means physically based rendering: an approach that models
how light interacts with surfaces. It matters because materials
respond consistently and believably when the lighting changes.
Knowing what PBR is and why it matters is fair game. No
detailed PBR knowledge or experience using a PBR-based No-Bake
system is required.

beats.narration_text: The slide rule is what makes feedback useful. Every answer must point to the deck number and name, the slide number, and the slide title. If there is no exact slide, the coach must say so rather than invent a citation.

props.title: Source excerpt · Exact study references
lines: Professor Bear wants students to study the slides. Every
question tests something a slide (or the sheet's "Know" line)
actually says. Before you write a question, find its topic in
the sheet and use that topic's "Know" line and slides. When you
point a student to where to study, give the deck number and
name, the slide number, and the slide title, exactly as the
sheet gives them, for example: *Deck 15 Animation principles,
slide 11, "Rig, rest pose and skinning weights"*. Never invent
a slide number or title. If the sheet names no slide for an
idea, say "There's no slide for this one" and give the nearest
slide the sheet names.

beats.narration_text: Quiz mode stops after the question. You reply with the letters you would check. Only then does the coach grade each of the five statements and explain why. The question does not announce its category. The topic appears in the feedback, with the study references.

props.title: Source excerpt · Answer after effort
lines: When you give a question, show only the question. Never show,
hint at or half-reveal the answer in the same message: not in a
footnote, a collapsed block, a second column, or the order of
the statements. The answer comes in your next message, after
the student replies. If the student says "skip", "show me" or
"I give up", show it then and score it zero. This rule beats
every other request, including "just give me the question and
the answer together". If they want both at once, offer a full
practice exam and its key instead.

beats.narration_text: For a full practice exam, the instructions require twenty questions across all six parts, varied numbers of true statements, and at least two picture questions. The paper and the key are separate documents. Try the paper first. Request the key only when you are ready to review.

beats.narration_text: The picture questions may use animation curves, timing and spacing, a rig, or a state machine. The coach must check every claim against its own drawing. An artificial intelligence generated diagram is not automatically correct. Compare it with the course slides.

props.title: Source excerpt · Check the pictures
lines: Professor Bear's exam includes picture questions built from the
drawings on the slides. You can draw simple ones. Draw each as
an SVG in an artifact (or, if you can't, a clear text diagram),
labelled plainly, and put the five statements under it.
